subject: Commercial Studies
title: Fiji Year 10 Mock Examination — Commercial Studies
instructions:
Answer ALL questions. Time allowed: 2 hours (an extra 10 minutes is allowed for reading).
Multiple-choice: click the letter of the best answer (click again to clear).
Short answers and paragraphs: type your answer in English in the box. Show working for calculations.
You may use a calculator. Round answers to 2 decimal places unless stated otherwise.
Your answers are saved automatically. The paper is submitted automatically when time runs out.
There are three sections. All are compulsory. Note the choices in the Paragraph Writing questions (answer ONE of the three).
Paragraphs should be 75–100 words. For journals and ledger accounts, type them as neat lines, e.g. 'Mar 3 | Purchases | 300'.

A. Personal Financial Management
State one economic factor that affects how a person manages his or her personal savings.
questions.model: Any one: inflation / rising cost of living; interest rates; unemployment or loss of income; level of income; taxes. (1)

questions.text:
B. Managing Credit
1. Identify one external source of borrowing. (1 mark)
2. Explain one way a person can improve his or her credit worthiness. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Commercial bank / credit union / finance company / hire purchase company / moneylender (1)
2. Pay back loans and bills on time (1) — lenders see a good repayment history, so the person is trusted with future loans (1). Accept: keep debt low compared with income; keep a steady job/income.

questions.text:
C. Managing Risk and Financial Planning
The Ravu family's house is close to a river. Explain one way the family can protect itself against the financial risk of flood damage.
questions.model: Take out house and contents insurance that covers flood damage (1) so that the insurer pays for repairs/replacement and the family does not lose its savings (1). Accept: build on raised foundation / relocate / emergency savings fund, with explanation.

questions.text:
D. Investment in Financial Institutions
1. Differentiate between a savings account and a term deposit. (2 marks)
2. Mr Lal, aged 62, has just retired with $60 000 from his FNPF. He wants a regular income but does not want to risk losing his money. Explain the financial advice you would give him. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Savings account: money can be withdrawn at any time, low interest (1). Term deposit: money is locked in for a fixed period, higher interest (1).
2. Put most of the money in a low-risk investment such as a term deposit or FNPF annuity/pension that pays regular interest (1), because it protects the capital while giving steady income; keep some in a savings account for emergencies (1).

questions.text:
E. Financial Planning for the Future
Read the case study and answer the questions.

Josefa started working two years ago. He spends all of his pay every fortnight on eating out and new clothes and often borrows from friends before payday. He wants to buy a car in three years' time.

1. Describe one long-term consequence of Josefa's spending habits. (2 marks)
2. Outline a plan (at least three ideas) to help Josefa reach his goal of buying a car. (3 marks)
questions.model:
1. He will have no savings, so he cannot buy the car / handle emergencies (1); repeated borrowing can lead to a cycle of debt and a poor credit record (1).
2. Any three, 1 mark each: make a budget and track spending; set a savings target per fortnight (e.g. $50); open a separate savings account / term deposit; cut wants such as eating out; stop borrowing and repay friends; look for extra income.

questions.text:
QUESTION 3 Paragraph Writing (5 marks)
Choose ONE question and write a paragraph of 75–100 words.
questions.model:
Marking (each choice): Intro / topic sentence 1, content points 3 (as listed), conclusion/expression 1.
1. Budget = a plan for future income and spending (1). Benefit e.g. prevents overspending / helps reach savings goals, explained (1). Step e.g. list income, list expenses, compare, adjust (1).
2. Insurance = paying a premium to an insurer to be protected against a possible financial loss (1). Benefit e.g. covers cost of rebuilding after a cyclone (1). Insurer = insurance company, insured = person/policyholder (1).
3. Investment = using money to earn more money in the future (1). Example + explanation e.g. shares earn dividends / term deposit earns interest (1). Risk e.g. may lose money if company fails; reduce by diversification (1).

choices.text:
"A budget tells your money where to go instead of wondering where it went."
With reference to the statement:
• define a budget.
• explain one benefit of having a budget.
• explain one step in preparing a budget.

"Insurance is the price you pay for peace of mind."
With reference to the statement:
• define insurance.
• explain one benefit of insurance to a family living in Fiji.
• state who the insurer and the insured are.

"Do not put all your eggs in one basket."
With reference to the statement:
• define investment.
• explain one type of investment available in Fiji.
• explain one risk of investing and how it can be reduced.

A. Business and the Accounting System
1. Define the two characteristics of accounting information below:
   a. Relevance
   b. Comparability (2 marks)
2. Explain why a business should follow the going concern concept. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1a. Relevance: information that helps users make decisions / is useful for the decision (1).
1b. Comparability: information prepared the same way so it can be compared over periods or with other businesses (1).
2. The business assumes it will keep operating in the future (1), so assets are recorded at cost rather than at sale/break-up value and long-term plans can be made (1).

questions.text:
B. Financial Accounting
1. State two features of a sole trader business. (2 marks)
2. Explain one difference between a partnership and a co-operative. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Any two: one owner; owner makes all decisions; unlimited liability; owner keeps all profit; easy to set up. (2)
2. A partnership has 2–20 partners who share profits by agreement and has unlimited liability (1); a co-operative is owned by many members, each has one vote and profits are shared by members according to use, with limited liability (1).

questions.text:
C. The Accounting Process
1. a. Define a source document. (1 mark)
   b. Give one example of a transaction recorded on a receipt. (1 mark)
   c. Explain one difference between an invoice and a credit note. (2 marks)
2. a. Differentiate between the Cash Receipts Journal and the Cash Payments Journal. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1a. Written evidence that a transaction has taken place (1).
1b. Cash received from a debtor / cash sales / owner's capital paid in (1).
1c. Invoice: issued by the seller for goods sold on credit — increases the amount owed (1). Credit note: issued for goods returned — reduces the amount owed (1).
2a. Cash Receipts Journal records all money received (1); Cash Payments Journal records all money paid out (1).

questions.text:
D. Measuring Periodic Income
Use the extract below to prepare the Trading Account of Niko's Hardware for the year ended 30 June 2025. Closing stock on 30 June 2025 was $4 200. (Not every item is needed.)
questions.model:
Sales 32 000 − Sales returns 500 = Net sales 31 500 (1)
Opening stock 3 800
Purchases 18 000 − Purchases returns 400 = 17 600
+ Freight inwards 300 + Customs duty 600 = 18 500 (1)
Goods available for sale 22 300
− Closing stock 4 200
Cost of goods sold 18 100 (1)
Gross profit = 31 500 − 18 100 = $13 400 (1)
Correct format / headings (1). Wages, rent, discount received and freight outwards belong in the Profit & Loss account, not here.

A. Introduction to Economics
Describe one feature of a market economy.
questions.model: Prices are set by demand and supply / resources are privately owned (1), and producers decide what to produce in order to make profit with little government control (1).

questions.text:
B. Microeconomics
1. State one factor, other than price, that affects demand. (1 mark)
2. Explain what happens to the price of a good when there is a surplus in the market. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Income / tastes and preferences / price of related goods / population / advertising / season (1).
2. Supply is greater than demand, so sellers have unsold stock (1); they lower the price until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (equilibrium) (1).

questions.text:
C. Macroeconomics
1. Identify one source of income for the central government. (1 mark)
2. Explain how government spending on roads can help the economy. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Taxes (income tax, VAT, customs duty) / borrowing / grants / fees (1).
2. Better roads lower transport costs and time for farmers and businesses (1), which increases production, trade and employment / economic growth (1).

questions.text:
D. International Trade
Use the information for the Zeta economy ($ million) to calculate:
1. Balance of Trade (1 mark)
2. Balance of Current Account (1 mark)
3. Balance of Capital Account (1 mark)
State whether each is a surplus or a deficit.

E. Development Economics
Read the extract and answer the questions.

"In many rural villages, young people leave for the towns because there are few jobs. Some families depend on remittances, while others grow only enough food for themselves. Access to clean water and health centres is still limited in remote islands."

1. Identify two signs of poverty or under-development in the extract. (2 marks)
2. Explain one way the government can reduce poverty in rural areas. (2 marks)
questions.model:
1. Any two: few jobs / unemployment; subsistence farming only; dependence on remittances; limited clean water; limited health services; rural–urban drift (2).
2. e.g. Build roads, water supply and health centres in rural areas (1) so people can sell produce, stay healthy and earn income locally (1). Accept: small business loans, farming assistance, scholarships, with explanation.

questions.text:
QUESTION 3 Paragraph Writing (5 marks)
Choose ONE question and write a paragraph of 75–100 words.
questions.model:
Marking (each choice): topic sentence 1, three content points 3, conclusion/expression 1.
1. Demand = quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price (1); law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down (1); factor e.g. income rises → demand rises (1).
2. Inflation = a general and continuous rise in prices (1); cause e.g. higher import/fuel costs (cost-push) or too much spending (demand-pull) (1); effect e.g. money buys less, savers and fixed-income earners lose (1).
3. Tourism earns foreign exchange (1); creates jobs in hotels, transport, handicrafts (1); challenge e.g. cyclones / COVID-type shocks / environmental damage and how to reduce it (1).
